title: Security & Compliance: RBAC, Audit Logging, Data Residency, SDLC, Incident Response, Evidence Workflows, and Risk Exceptions
author: Aisha Patel
body:
Overview

This document consolidates Redwood Inference's operational policies and workflows for: role-based access control (RBAC) and authentication, audit logging, data residency and retention, secure software development lifecycle (SDLC) controls, security-focused incident response procedures, compliance evidence collection and submission workflows, and the formal process for risk exceptions. It is intended for engineers, security reviewers, product owners, and audit/compliance teams.

Scope

Applies to:
- Hosted API control plane and customer-facing consoles
- Dedicated and Private deployment control planes (management plane)
- Internal developer tools, CI/CD pipelines, and build artifacts
- Audit and evidence storage systems used for compliance reporting

Principles

- Least privilege by default: grant the minimum permission required and require explicit justification for elevation.
- Immutable evidence: audit logs, signed artifacts, and tamper-resistant evidence are primary sources for audits.
- Clear ownership: every control has a documented owner and reviewer cadence.
- Repeatable workflows: evidence and exception processes must be scripted where possible.

1) RBAC and Authentication

Overview: RBAC is enforced across Redwood services using a central authorization service (internal name: rbac-gateway). Authentication is provided by the corporate identity provider (IdP) backed by SSO (SAML/OIDC) with MFA required for all interactive access.

Key controls:
- Roles: defined at three layers — Platform Admin, Service Owner, Developer, Read-Only Auditor, Support Engineer. Role definitions live in the rbac-gateway repo and are the source of truth.
- Time-bound elevated access: emergency or task-based elevated roles must use just-in-time (JIT) access via Vault/Access Manager with an approval ticket. Default lease: 8 hours.
- Service-to-service auth: mutual TLS or mTLS with short-lived certificates issued by internal PKI; rotating certificates automated via cert-manager.
- MFA: enforced for all human logins; hardware tokens required for staff with privileged roles.

Procedures (high level):
1. Request access via Access Portal (link in internal tools). Include justification, duration, and owner.
2. Reviewer (service owner) approves or rejects within 48 hours.
3. Provisioning is automated; access events emit audit entries (see section 2).

Ownership and SLOs:
- RBAC policy owner: security-policy@redwood.com (team: security).
- Provisioning latency SLO: 95% of approved access is provisioned within 5 minutes of approval.

2) Audit Logging

Overview: Comprehensive audit logging is required for authentication, authorization decisions, administrative actions, data exports, and changes to customer configuration. Logs are routed to the central Audit Lake (internal name: audit-lake) and retained according to classification.

What is logged:
- Auth events: login success/failure, SSO assertions, MFA failures, token issuance/revocation.
- Authorization decisions: allow/deny with policy id and rationale.
- Administrative actions: role changes, policy edits, JIT approvals, secrets rotation.
- Data access/export: queries returning >1k rows, bulk exports, and customer data movement across regions.

Alerting thresholds (examples):
- Authentication failure spike: >20 failures for same account within 10 minutes -> P2 alert.
- Unexpected policy change: role binding changed outside the approved RBAC pipeline -> P1 alert.
- Large export: data export >100GB or export to external storage -> P1 alert and automatic hold.

Audit log retention (table):
- System logs (infrastructure): 1 year (hot), 5 years (cold)
- Auth & RBAC logs: 7 years
- Customer access logs (per customer SLA): configurable; default 3 years
- PCI/Regulated data access records: 7 years

Integrity and access:
- Logs are immutable-writes via append-only storage with HMAC chain linking.
- Access to audit-lake requires Auditor role and is logged separately.

3) Data Residency & Retention

Residency model:
- Customer data at rest is co-located to supported regions depending on customer contract and product tier (Hosted: multi-region with controls; Dedicated/Private: per-customer VPC).
- Cross-region transfers require documented customer consent and encryption-in-transit with TLS 1.2+ and internal approvals.

Retention policy (standard defaults):
- Raw customer input/outputs (user prompt & model response): default 90 days; can be configured per-customer down to 0 days for strict customers.
- Derived embeddings, model telemetry: 365 days by default, aggregate metrics may be retained longer (5 years) with obfuscation.
- Backups & snapshots: encrypted; retention per backup policy table (30/90/365 depending on resource).

Requirements for regulated customers:
- Cryptographic key management integrated with customer KMS (bring-your-own-key) where required.
- Logical separation of logs and telemetry for customers subject to data residency laws.

4) Secure SDLC (security controls in engineering lifecycle)

Mandatory gates:
- Design review: all systems handling customer data must pass a security design review (checklist includes data flows, threat model, and key management).
- Static analysis: PRs for services in scope must include SAST scan results with no critical findings.
- Dependency policy: denylist-based CI checks; vulnerabilities with CVSS >= 7 require approval and milestone for remediation.
- Secrets management: no secrets in code; CI injects secrets from Vault.

Release controls:
- Canary and progressive rollout for control plane and serving runtime changes. Automations must include automatic rollback on error rate regressions exceeding thresholds.
- Release evidence: signed release manifest, build provenance (attested by CI), test/eval results linked to manifest.

5) Incident Response — Security Procedures

Activation criteria:
- Confirmed compromise of credentials, data exfiltration, or control plane integrity issue -> incident declared.

Tiered response tasks (summary):
1. Triage & containment: identify impacted services/customers, revoke affected credentials, and isolate compromised hosts.
2. Evidence preservation: snapshot volatile memory if needed, preserve audit-lake subset, and collect signed manifests.
3. Communication: notify internal stakeholders, legal, and customer-success triage teams per customer contract.
4. Remediation & recovery: patch/roll forward, rotate keys, and validate via forensics.
5. Post-incident review: produce a postmortem with root cause, timeline, impact, and remediation steps.

Playbook highlights:
- All incident actions must be recorded in the incident timeline and appended to the incident evidence bundle in audit-lake.
- For incidents affecting customer data residency or export, legal must approve notification language before customer outreach.

6) Compliance Evidence Workflows

Purpose: Provide repeatable, auditable artifacts for internal or third-party audits (SOC2, ISO27001, GDPR assessments).

Primary evidence artifacts (examples):
- RBAC policy history and signed approvals.
- Audit log extracts (signed with HMAC and time-window metadata).
- Build & release manifests with CI attestations.
- Vulnerability scan reports and remediation tickets.
- Data retention configuration per customer and deletion proof.

Workflow (high level):
1. Evidence request received via Compliance Portal (ticketing system).
2. Security evidence owner identifies artifacts and collects signed extracts.
3. Evidence packaged into a read-only evidence bundle with index.json and HMAC signatures.
4. Compliance reviewer signs off; bundle stored in Evidence Vault with access audit.

Time expectations: standard internal requests are fulfilled within 5 business days; urgent regulator requests targeted within 48 hours.

7) Risk & Exceptions

When to use: Exceptions are required when a control cannot be met for technical, operational, or customer reasons (e.g., a customer requires cross-region exports contradicting default residency).

Exception process:
1. Submit an Exception Request with technical justification, duration, compensating controls, and owner.
2. Security reviews for technical risk and product/legal review for contractual/regulatory impact.
3. Risk Committee (monthly) approves high-risk exceptions or escalates to CTO/CISO for approval.
4. Approved exceptions produce a signed Exception Record stored in Evidence Vault and are time-bound with automatic reminders before expiration.

Compensating controls examples:
- Additional logging and frequent access reviews.
- Network isolation and encrypted tunnels with restricted egress.
- Customer-signed waiver and higher service-level monitoring.

8) Operational Runbooks & Playbooks

Links: runbooks are available in the eng-sre and eng-infra directories. Key runbooks include:
- audit-lake-incident-playbook: steps for investigating log integrity alerts.
- rbac-policy-change-playbook: procedure for emergency policy rollback.
- data-export-hold-playbook: automated hold and legal notification flow.

9) Appendix: Example Commands & Evidence Templates

CLI snippets (examples):
- Export signed audit log window (example):
  curl -H \"Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN\" \"https://audit-lake.internal/api/v1/exports?start=2027-02-01T00:00:00Z&end=2027-02-28T23:59:59Z\" 
  # Response includes signed_bundle_url and HMAC header

- Request a JIT role: (pseudo)
  jq -n '{role: "service-admin", duration: "8h", justification: "DB migration"}' | \
  http POST https://access-portal.internal/requests Authorization:\"Bearer $USER_TOKEN\"

Evidence index template (index.json example described):
- bundle_id: string (UUID)
- created_at: ISO8601 timestamp
- artifacts: list of artifact descriptors (name, path, sha256, hmac)
- approver_signatures: list of approver ids and signature blob
